::: {.callout-tip}
## Here you will learn

How to use a coarse-grained subsample of target pixels - or "landmarks" -
to increase computational performance with minimal loss in accuracy.

:::

In this notebook we demonstrate the use of landmarks with the `coarse_graining`
function to reduce the computational demands in ConScape, see main text of
details and discussion.

# Data import

See notebook [getting started](/notebooks/nbk_getting_started.qmd) for a 'basic
workflow' to learn about data import and the creation of a ConScape `Grid`:

```{julia}
using ConScape
using Rasters
using ArchGDAL
using Statistics
using CairoMakie
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
datadir = joinpath(dirname(pathof(ConScape)), "..", "data")
```

```{julia}
paths = (steplikelihood=joinpath(datadir, "mov_prob_1000.asc"),
         quality=joinpath(datadir, "hab_qual_1000.asc"))
rast = RasterStack(paths; missingval=NaN)
mask!(rast; with=rast) # Self masking
```

# Coarse graining

Internally, target qualities can be represented by a sparse matrix. This means 
that habitat of quality zero is not explicitly stored in the matrix, which
reduces the memory footprint in case of matrices with many zeros. 

We can further increase the sparseness of this matrix to reduce the computational
requirements in terms of processing time. 

`ConScape.Problem` has a `grain` argument to control the coase of aggregation.
It does so by summing the target qualities of all pixels and assigning this value 
to the center pixel, while setting all other cells to zero. When running 
`init` or `solve` on a `MovementMode` like `RSP`, `grain` can be passed as a
keyword, that will be used to construct a `Problem` internally.

The idea is thus to connect pixels from a higher resolution
source map to a lower resolution target map. The benefit of this approach
compared to, for instance, using lower resolution maps in general is that
movement paths are still represented with a high resolution. 

The main assumption this is that all high-resolution pixels within a coarse pixel 
are equally well connected to the source pixel as the high-resolution pixel at the 
center of the coarse pixel. This assumption will be more difficult to meet with 
increasing number of pixels aggregated and with increasing heterogeneity in the landscape.

We will now investigate how the estimation of the amount of connected habitat
and the movement flow are affected by this coarse graining of the target pixels.

## Connected habitat and coarse graining

We compute the amount of connected habitat or functionality for each pixel using
the expected cost distance and an exponential decay for both the high-resolution
and low-resolution target qualities:

```{julia}
theta = 1.0
rsp = RSP(; theta, distance_transformation=x -> exp(-x / 75))
fh = solve(ConScapeProblem(FunctionalHabitat(), rsp), rast) 
fh_coarse = solve(ConScapeProblem(FunctionalHabitat(), rsp), rast; grain=20)
```

The reduction in computation is substantial. The processing time goes from 16 to
0.05 seconds and the memory requirements from 2.5 Gb to 18 Mb by aggregating $20
\times 20$ pixels into a single pixel. Obviously, the reduction in computation
will be less with lower numbers of pixels aggregated. However, even merging as
few as 2 or 3 pixels will result in substantial reductions in computation
(respectively 2.6 and 1.2 seconds of processing time, and 503 Mb and 232 Mb of
memory). 


```{julia}
#| fig-cap: Comparison of functional habitat without and with landmarks.
#| fig-subcap: 
#|   - "a"
#|   - "b"
#| layout-ncol: 2

display(plot(fh; axis=(; title="Complete")))
display(plot(fh_coarse; axis=(; title="Landmark-based")))
```

Compare the computation based on all pixels versus the one based on landmarks
and we see they are highly similar.

Hence, the correlation between these values is:

```{julia}
cor(filter(x -> !isnan(x), fh), filter(x -> !isnan(x), fh_coarse))
```

Clearly, the estimation of the ranking of source pixels based upon their
functional connectivity to target pixels is relatively little affected by the
aggregation of these target pixels. 

When we look at the change in the amount of connected habitat in the landscape:

```{julia}
sqrt(sum(filter(x -> !isnan(x), fh_coarse))) / sqrt(sum(filter(x -> !isnan(x), fh)))
```

There is some under-estimation, however, note that we used a substantial level
of coarse graining (i.e. $20 \times 20$). We now investigate how the accuracy
changes for different levels of coarse graining.

Compute both the correlation between pixel-level and landscape-level amount
of connnected habitat over a range of aggregation levels (from 1, no
aggregation, to 50):

```{julia}
coarseness = [1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 15, 20, 50]
time_fh_grains = map(coarseness) do grain
    time = @elapsed begin
        fh = solve(ConScapeProblem(FunctionalHabitat(), rsp), rast; grain)
    end
    time, fh
end
```

Calculate sums and correlations with non-aggregated outputs:

```{julia}
time_grains = first.(time_fh_grains)
fh_grains = last.(time_fh_grains)
skipnan(xs) = filter(x -> !isnan(x), xs)
est_fh_grains = sum.(skipnan.(fh_grains))
cor_fh_grains = cor.((skipnan(fh),), skipnan.(fh_grains))
```

```{julia}
#| fig-cap: The correlation between the full and landmark-based habitat functionality in function of the level of 'coarse graining'.
fig = Figure()
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1])
ax2 = Axis(fig[2, 1])
scatterlines!(ax1, coarseness, est_fh_grains; color=:black, label="Estimated connected habitat")
scatterlines!(ax2, coarseness, cor_fh_grains; label="Correlation")    
scatterlines!(ax2, coarseness, time_grains ./ first(time_grains); label="Relative computation time")
axislegend(ax1; position=:rc)
axislegend(ax2; position=:rc)
fig
```

The ranking of source pixels based on their functional connectivity to
high-quality target pixels, is hardly affected by aggregation. Aggregating less
than $10 \times 10$ pixels results in a virtual identical ranking, whereas even
sever levels of aggregation ($50 \times 50$) still result in a correlation above
$0.98$. 

However the loss in accuracy is a bit more pronounced for the
amount of connnected habitat.

We can see in our example that aggregating less than 10 pixels will result in
less than 1% drop in estimated amount of connected habitat, but increasing the
level of aggregation will result in an accelerating underestimation of the
actual amount of connected habitat.

# Betweenness and coarse graining

We compute the betweenness or movement flow for each pixel for both the
high-resolution and low-resolution ($20 \times 20$) target qualities, first for
the quality weighted version:

```{julia}
qbetw = solve(ConScapeProblem(Betweenness(QualityWeighted()), rsp), rast)
qbetw_coarse = solve(ConScapeProblem(Betweenness(QualityWeighted()), rsp), rast; grain=20)
```

```{julia}
cor(skipnan(qbetw), skipnan(qbetw_coarse))
```

Although, there is still a high correlation, this drop in accuracy is actually
perceivable in the maps:

```{julia}
#| fig-cap: Comparison of quality-weighted betweenness without and with landmarks.
#| fig-subcap: 
#|   - "a"
#|   - "b"
#| layout-ncol: 2

display(plot(qbetw; axis=(; title="Complete")))
display(plot(qbetw_coarse; axis=(; title="Landmark-based")))
```

We found similar results for the quality and proximity weighted version of the
betweenness: 

```{julia}
mbetw = solve(ConScapeProble(MovementFlow(), rsp), rast)
mbetw_coarse = solve(ConScapeProble(MovementFlow(), rsp), rast; grain=20)
```

```{julia}
cor(skipnan(mbetw), skipnan(mbetw_coarse))
```

```{julia}
#| fig-cap: Comparison of proximity-weighted betweenness without and with landmarks.
#| fig-subcap: 
#|   - "a"
#|   - "b"
#| layout-ncol: 2

display(plot(mbetw; axis=(; title="Complete")))
display(plot(mbetw_coarse; axis=(; title="Landmark-based")))
```

As commented above, a $20 \times 20$ aggregation of pixels is quite a high level
of compression. Let's now see how the accuracy changes with changing levels of
aggregation.

```{julia}
betw = (
    qbetw=Betweenness(QualityWeighted()),
    mbetw=Betweenness(QualityAndProximityWeighted())
)
betw_grains = map(coarseness) do grain
    solve(ConScapeProblem(betw, rsp), rast; grain)
end
```

```{julia}
qbetw_grains = map(g -> skipnan(g.qbetw), betw_grains)
mbetw_grains = map(g -> skipnan(g.mbetw), betw_grains)
est_qbetw_grains = sum.(qbetw_grains)
est_mbetw_grains = sum.(mbetw_grains)
cor_qbetw_grains = cor.((skipnan(qbetw),), qbetw_grains)
cor_mbetw_grains = cor.((skipnan(mbetw),), mbetw_grains)
```

```{julia}
#| fig-cap: The correlation between the full and landmark-based betweenness in function of the level of 'coarse graining'.

p = scatterlines(coarseness, cor_qbetw_grains; 
    alpha=0.7, label="Quality-weighted betweenness"
)
scatterlines!(p.axis, coarseness, cor_mbetw_grains; 
    alpha=0.7, label="Quality and proximity-weighted betweenness"
)
axislegend(p.axis; position=:lb)
p.figure
```

We see that the level of accuracy is good for levels of aggregation below 10,
but starts to drop off rather rapidly above this. 

## Summary

The keyword `grain` in useful tool to reduce the computational demands of
dealing with high-resolution landscapes by connecting a high-resolution map of
source pixels to a lower resolution map of target pixels. 

Unfortunately, the computational benefits come at the cost of a loss in
accuracy. We found for our example that aggregation levels below 10 led to a
substantial benefit in terms of computation with minimal loss in accuracy. We
suggest that researchers explore how the accuracy changes in their landscape
with changing levels of aggregation. 

Windowing the landscape is an alternative approach to reduce computational
demands, see [windowing](/notebooks/nbk_windowing.qmd).
